units.title: Replica serving and tensor-parallel inference shapes and collectives
outcomes: Distinguish independent serving replicas from ranks cooperating on one forward pass, including their request-level fault domains.
Derive local MLP and attention projection shapes for a tensor-parallel serving plan.
Place forward collectives and explain why added memory capacity need not reduce small-batch latency.
units.why: A router distributes requests across replicas; tensor parallelism distributes one request's model work across ranks. Confusing the two gives the wrong capacity estimate and the wrong recovery boundary.

next.note: Turn the shard shapes into per-rank ownership and memory budgets.

study.title: Replicas versus model shards
study.locator: Chapter 7, Data Parallelism, printed pp. 243 to 245; Tensor Parallelism and Pipeline Parallelism, printed pp. 245 to 250
study.depth: Read the replica and TP paths now. Leave the pipeline decision path for the next unit; do not run the multi-GPU launch snippet.

study.title: The paired column and row shards
study.locator: Module 09, Tensor parallelism: split inside the layer - The MLP block and The attention block
study.depth: Stop before Communication volume. Two reductions per layer describes this replicated-activation dense forward schedule, not every TP implementation.

focus: Reuse Collective contracts and the latency-bandwidth cost model. Serving replicas do not synchronize gradients; a replica can itself contain a TP group.

For input \(X\) of shape \(T 	imes h\), column-shard the first MLP weight of shape \(h 	imes f\), then row-shard the second of shape \(f 	imes h\). Each local intermediate has shape \(T 	imes f/n\) for divisible width and \(n\) ranks.
An elementwise activation stays local between these shards. The second projection produces same-shaped partial outputs that sum, not concatenate. Add a replicated output bias once after summation.
Attention head shards can compute independently before the output projection reduction. KV-head replication and vocabulary-parallel output paths need separate ownership accounting.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive a bias-free two-rank ReLU MLP with input shape \(2 	imes 4\), first weight shape \(4 	imes 6\) and second weight shape \(6 	imes 4\). Give each rank three intermediate features, sum its partial output, and check against the unsharded MLP on CPU using small deterministic float64 tensors. State a numerical tolerance rather than demanding bitwise equality.
traps: Counting replicas as additional memory for a single request. Each independent replica needs the full model and its own admitted KV state.
Calling every column-sharded output an all-reduce. Disjoint output features concatenate; row-sharded dot-product contributions sum.
Promising a latency speedup from rank count. Smaller kernels, startup costs and dependencies can consume the extra compute or memory bandwidth.

selfTest.q: Does inference replica serving require the training gradient all-reduce?
selfTest.a: No. Independent requests run forward passes against fixed weights. Shared routing or cache metadata is a separate control-plane concern.

selfTest.q: Why can the first projection's activation remain local?
selfTest.a: Each rank owns complete values for its output features, and ReLU acts independently on each feature. No partial sum is needed before that activation.

selfTest.q: What shape does each second-projection partial have in the reproduce example?
selfTest.a: \(2 	imes 4\). Each rank multiplies a \(2 	imes 3\) intermediate by its \(3 	imes 4\) weight rows; the two partials sum to the full output.

selfTest.q: Can replicas lower endpoint latency without making the forward pass faster?
selfTest.a: Yes. Distributing arrivals can reduce queueing. It does not shorten the isolated forward service time on an unchanged replica.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: servelab's replica and TP plans, local-shape ledger and differential checks against an unsharded forward pass.
units.stopWhen: Your paired-shard MLP matches the unsharded reference within the stated tolerance, and your diagram separates replica routing from TP collectives and their fault domains.

fit.note: The book's replica and sharding sections and Module 09's paired MLP cover the serving distinction and forward shapes; servelab supplies CPU differential practice.

units.title: Pipeline bubbles, expert-parallel MoE and context parallelism in serving
outcomes: Derive a forward-only pipeline timeline and identify the concurrency and stage balance needed to fill it.
Map MoE dispatch and combine to serving ranks, preserving the selected experts and routing weights.
Distinguish layer, expert, head and context-position partitioning, including the communication exact attention still needs.
units.why: PP, EP and context parallelism partition different axes. Their serving value depends on available concurrency, expert skew and context length, not just whether the model fits.

study.title: A forward pipeline bubble exercise
study.locator: Day 17, Pipeline Parallelism: layer blocks + the bubble; Try These Experiments, item 4, PP bubble break-even
study.depth: Only this timeline and exercise. Assume equal forward stage times and independent microbatches; do not import a training backward schedule.

focus: Reuse All-to-all and MoE dispatch, combine and load balance. In serving, small decode batches can expose startup and hot-expert delay even when the aggregate dispatch byte count is small.

With \(p\) equal stages, \(m\) ready independent microbatches and stage time \(t\), a transfer-free forward pipeline finishes in \((m+p-1)t\). Idle fraction is \((p-1)/(m+p-1)\); autoregressive feedback and uneven stage times invalidate that simple schedule.

Expert placement changes which assignments cross a slow link. Replicating the same expert preserves its function; changing top-k choices or overflow semantics does not automatically preserve model quality.

Context parallelism partitions positions; TP commonly partitions heads. Exact global attention still incorporates every permitted position using communicated KV blocks or partial softmax statistics. Sequence parallelism can instead mean partitioning intermediate activations around TP - state the axis, not just the acronym.
units.reproduce: Draw the transfer-free forward timeline for four equal 2 ms stages and eight ready independent microbatches. Recover a 22 ms makespan and idle fraction \(3/11\). Then add the dependency from the final sampled token to the same request's next decode pass and explain why eight successive tokens of one request cannot fill the pipeline like eight independent microbatches.
traps: Using a full-training pipeline bubble formula for forward-only inference, or treating future tokens of one request as already available microbatches.
Placing paired hot experts together without checking compute imbalance. Fewer remote bytes can still leave one rank on the critical path.
Summing locally normalized attention outputs. Each slice has a different softmax normalizer; exact merging must reweight them.

selfTest.q: Does PP make four equal stages execute one isolated request simultaneously?
selfTest.a: No. Its activations traverse all four stages in order. Other independent requests can occupy the remaining stages; the isolated request retains the full dependency chain.

selfTest.q: Why is an expert replica different from rerouting to another expert?
selfTest.a: A replica computes the same expert function with the same weights. A different expert generally computes a different function, changing the model output.

selfTest.q: Do position shards let exact causal attention ignore distant earlier positions?
selfTest.a: No. Those positions remain legal keys. Their contributions must reach the query through KV exchange or a correctly normalized partial-result merge.

selfTest.q: What does a slow PP stage do to steady-state capacity?
selfTest.a: It limits the rate at which microbatches can leave the pipeline. More stages or a low average stage time cannot remove that bottleneck.
